content: Cattle, sheep, and goats are the primary reservoirs of Coxiella burnetii. However, the infection has also been observed in a wide range of other animals, including other livestock species and domesticated pets. In most cases, C. burnetii does not cause clinical disease in these animals, although it has been associated with abortion in goats and sheep. The bacteria are excreted in the milk, urine, and feces of infected animals. During birthing, the organisms are shed in extremely high numbers within the amniotic fluids and placenta. These bacteria are highly resistant to heat, drying, and many common disinfectants, which allows them to survive in the environment for extended periods. Human infection typically occurs through inhalation of airborne particles contaminated with dried placental material, birth fluids, or excreta from infected animals. This contamination often occurs in barnyard dust. Humans are highly susceptible to the disease, and only a small number of organisms are required to cause infection. Ingestion of contaminated milk, followed by regurgitation and aspiration of the contaminated material, is a less common route of transmission. Other modes of transmission, such as tick bites or human-to-human spread, are rare. The incubation period for Q fever is generally 2 to 3 weeks. The most common presentation includes flu-like symptoms with a sudden onset of fever, which typically lasts 7 to 14 days. Other symptoms include malaise, profuse sweating, severe headache, muscle pain (myalgia), joint pain, loss of appetite, upper respiratory symptoms, dry cough, pleuritic chest pain, chills, confusion, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. In some cases, the disease can progress to atypical pneumonia, which may lead to life-threatening acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). These severe symptoms usually develop within the first 4 to 5 days of infection. Less commonly, Q fever can cause granulomatous hepatitis, which presents with symptoms such as malaise, fever, liver enlargement (hepatomegaly), right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and jaundice (icterus). Chronic Q fever is a more severe form of the disease and is often indistinguishable from endocarditis. It can develop months or even decades after the initial infection and is usually fatal if left untreated. With appropriate treatment, the mortality rate is reduced to approximately 10%. Chronic Q fever is more likely to occur in individuals with pre-existing valvular heart disease, vascular grafts, or those who are immunocompromised, such as transplant recipients or patients with cancer or chronic kidney disease. Up to 65% of individuals with chronic Q fever may die from the disease. Only about half of those infected with C. burnetii develop clinical illness. Acute Q fever typically begins with a sudden onset of high fever (up to 104–105°F), severe headache, general malaise, muscle pain, confusion, sore throat, chills, sweating, non-productive cough, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and chest pain. Fever usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks, and weight loss may persist for some time. Approximately 30–50% of symptomatic patients develop pneumonia, and many exhibit abnormal liver function tests, with some progressing to hepatitis. Most patients recover fully within several months without treatment, and the mortality rate for acute Q fever is only 1–2%. Chronic Q fever, defined as infection persisting for more than 6 months, is uncommon but significantly more serious. It can manifest as endocarditis, which may require transesophageal echocardiography for diagnosis. Chronic Q fever is often associated with pre-existing heart valve disease or vascular grafts. Other at-risk groups include transplant recipients, cancer patients, and those with chronic kidney disease. Chronic Q fever has a high mortality rate, with up to 65% of affected individuals succumbing to the disease. Q fever hepatitis is characterized by elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST). A definitive diagnosis requires a liver biopsy, which typically reveals fibrin ring granulomas. The incubation period for Q fever varies depending on the number of organisms that initially infect the patient, with higher bacterial loads leading to shorter incubation periods. Most patients become symptomatic within 2–3 weeks of exposure. Those who recover fully from the infection may develop lifelong immunity against reinfection. Common symptoms of Q fever include a dry, non-productive cough, fever, headache, joint pain (arthralgia), and muscle pain. Additional symptoms may include abdominal pain, chest pain, jaundice, and rash. Complications of Q fever are rare but can include osteomyelitis, encephalitis, chronic hepatitis, and pneumonia. In some cases, a heart infection (endocarditis) may develop, which can lead to severe symptoms or death if untreated.
